meeting_header:
Date: 2025-03-18
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Mateo Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dana Patel (Redwood CSM), Priya Rao (NimbusWorks SRE), Alan Kim (NimbusWorks Eng Mgr), Jess Tran (NimbusWorks ML Eng), Markus Lee (NimbusWorks Infra)
Recording: Fireflies auto-transcript
summary: POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscale for a 4-week POC. Discussed reserved GPU pool for baseline throughput, burst strategy for traffic spikes, and fallback policies for capacity exhaustion. Agreed success criteria: meet 95th p99-ish latency targets and throughput targets on production trace, cost envelope estimate for reserved vs hosted. Next steps: exchange traces, run benchmark, share pricing + POC worksheet.
transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna focus on sizing the POC and the autoscale/fallback story today. Uh, quick intros?
[00:12] Priya: Sure, I'm Priya, SRE at NimbusWorks. We're evaluating Redwood for customer-facing chat and code-assist flows. Latency is critical.
[00:20] Alan: Alan here, engineering manager, we'll own the integration and endpoint routing.
[00:25] Sophie: Great. Mateo is our SE who'll run benchmarks. Mateo?
[00:30] Mateo: Hi all, quick agenda: understand traffic profile, define POC success criteria, propose reserved capacity and burst plan, and outline benchmark steps.
[00:40] Jess: Quick note — we expect variable qps, daytime spikes from 50 to 600 qps across multiple tenants, median request is ~1.2k tokens, some long form at 6k tokens.
[00:50] Markus: Also we're on AWS in us-west-2 and need VPC peering for the private deployment side.
[00:55] Sophie: Got it. On the traffic: you said 600 qps at peak? Over what window?
[01:00] Jess: That's sustained for 10-20 minutes during business hours and occasional larger spikes for promos that can double that but only a few minutes.
[01:10] Mateo: Ok, good. So we need a baseline reserved pool sized for sustained throughput and a burst strategy for the short peaks. For the POC we usually recommend reserved GPUs to get stable performance and reproducible benchmarks.
[01:22] Priya: What's the minimum reserved you'd recommend for 600 qps?
[01:26] Mateo: Depends on model choice and batching. For example, with a Llama-2-13B style model quantized to int8 and a continuous batching config optimized for short chats, one A100-class equivalent GPU can handle about 80-120 concurrent streams depending on latency SLO. For 600 qps you might want 6-8 reserved GPUs as a starting point, plus a burst pool.
[01:44] Alan: That seems high — can you explain the math?
[01:47] Mateo: Sure. If median request is 1.2k tokens and average per-token latency is X, but more importantly tokens/sec matters. With batching we can amortize kernel overhead; however that adds a tradeoff — if we batch too long latency increases. For 95th percentile latency target of ~350-450ms for the initial POC, we size lower. So for 600 qps we estimate 6 reserved GPUs. If you relax latency to 600ms you can reduce GPUs by ~20-30%.
[02:12] Sophie: Also keep in mind we can route non-critical traffic to cheaper model variants — that's the fallback policy: when capacity constrained we fall back to a 7B quantized model or to a small hosted path.
[02:22] Priya: Fallback is important. We need to be explicit about consistency and quality regression monitoring during fallback.
[02:28] Mateo: Absolutely. For the POC we'll include quality regression checks tied to a prompt set. Canary rollout + automatic fallback if quality drops more than 3% on eval metrics or latency breaches the SLO.
[02:40] Jess: How does burst capacity work? Is it pre-warmed or cold start?
[02:45] Mateo: Two options: pre-warmed ephemeral GPUs or on-demand burst where we accept slightly higher latency (e.g., +200ms) for the first N seconds while kernels warm. For promos we recommend a small pre-warmed burst pool — say 2 GPUs — that sits idle but billing applies. Alternatively, you use an elastic burst to cloud spot capacity which is cheaper but riskier.
[03:03] Markus: For security reasons we prefer dedicated reserved capacity but can allow a limited hosted burst if it's in our VPC.
[03:09] Sophie: We can set up a hybrid: reserved pool in your VPC for baseline and a Redwood-managed burst pool with strict network controls and audit logs.
[03:18] Alan: What's the cost delta between reserved and burst?
[03:20] Sophie: Reserved is a monthly commit — typical POC reserved pricing examples we'll share in the worksheet. Burst on-demand is roughly 2-3x per-hour of reserved depending on GPU type. But amortizing across fewer hours for spikes may still be cheaper than overprovisioning reserved. We'll provide concrete SKUs.
[03:36] Priya: On fallback policies, can we do model variant fallback per-tenant? We have tiered customers.
[03:42] Mateo: Yes, routing policies can be per-tenant. You can pin premium tenants to a higher capacity or dedicated nodes, and fallback lower tiers to cheaper variants or even cached responses.
[03:51] Jess: Caching — do you do prefix/KV cache for repeated prompts?
[03:55] Mateo: Yes, automatic prefix caching, KV cache for session state — big win for chat. We'll need your session affinity patterns to size cache memory.
[04:05] Sophie: Let's capture success criteria explicitly. What does Nimbus consider a pass for the POC?
[04:10] Priya: Three things: 1) Latency: 95th percentile for interactive chat under 450ms for typical requests; 2) Throughput: meet 600 qps sustained for a 15 minute window with no errors; 3) Quality: model outputs within X BLEU-like or eval metric within 5% of current baseline on our prompt suite.
[04:28] Alan: Also SLOs around availability — 99.5% for API success rate during POC window.
[04:34] Mateo: Good. We'll instrument all metrics and run a 1-hour stress test and a 1-day soak during the POC. For benchmarking we ask you to provide a 7-day production trace and sample payloads. We'll replay both synthetic and real traces.
[04:48] Jess: We'll anonymize traces and include token distributions.
[04:51] Sophie: Timeline: typical POC is 4 weeks. Week 0-1: infra setup and capacity reservations and network (VPC peering). Week 2: run baseline benchmarks and tuning. Week 3: soak tests and quality evals. Week 4: run final acceptance benchmarks and review. Does that align?
[05:07] Priya: That works but we need the ability to extend if the soak reveals regressions.
[05:11] Sophie: Absolutely, we can add a 1-week extension as part of POC terms.
[05:14] Alan: On security/compliance: we need SOC 2 docs, audit logs, SAML/SSO, KMS integration for keys.
[05:21] Dana: We'll share our security pack. Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and audit logs — Mateo can walk through the private deployment checklist.
[05:29] Mateo: For VPC we need CIDR ranges and peering details. For KMS we do integration with customer-managed keys for model input/output encryption at rest.
[05:37] Markus: Network egress for burst pools — ensure traffic doesn't route outside allowed subnets.
[05:41] Mateo: We'll configure networking controls and dedicated subnets for private nodes.
[05:44] Sophie: For benchmarks, two asks from Nimbus: 1) which model family do you want us to benchmark against? 2) provide production trace.
[05:51] Jess: We'll decide between 13B and 70B; for cost reasons we prefer starting with 13B and evaluate quality delta.
[05:58] Mateo: Good plan. For 13B: expected GPUs for 600 qps baseline ~6 reserved; for 70B you'll need more like 12+ GPUs or heavier quantization. We'll include quantization profiles in the worksheet.
[06:12] Priya: How will you measure quality regression during fallback?
[06:15] Mateo: We run the prompt set through both variants and compute a delta on our eval metrics (ROUGE/semantic sim, custom scoring). We set alert thresholds and automatic rollback if metrics cross thresholds.
[06:25] Jess: And what about autoscale thresholds? We want to ensure scaling is predictable and doesn't thrash.
[06:30] Mateo: Use multiple levers: request queue depth, CPU/GPU utilization, and latency. We recommend calm backs off with hysteresis: scale up fast, scale down slower. For POC we'll use conservative thresholds and monitor.
[06:42] Sophie: Ok, recap of agreed items...
[06:45] Sophie: Redwood to send POC worksheet + pricing + SKU table and reserved vs burst cost examples.
[06:50] Sophie: Nimbus to provide 7-day production trace and confirm model family.
[06:54] Sophie: Mateo to schedule benchmark slot and prep test harness.
[06:58] Alan: We'll also sign the POC terms and provide network details for VPC peering.
[07:02] Sophie: Great. Any final questions?
[07:05] Priya: One more: can we have per-tenant throttles tied to contract tiers?
[07:09] Mateo: Yes, that's supported. We'll include an example routing policy.
[07:13] Sophie: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the worksheet and calendar invites for the benchmark.
[07:18] Alan: Thanks, bye.

Notes: transcript occasionally mis-heard product names (e.g., "K V cache" vs KV cache). There are short overlaps and filler words. References made to shared artifacts: POC worksheet (link to be provided), security pack (link to be provided), benchmark harness (SE will share GitHub gist).
